title: How Did People Build the Great Pyramid of Giza?
question: How did people build the Great Pyramid of Giza?
answer: Thousands of paid, skilled workers cut the stones with copper tools, hard stones and sand. They moved the stones by boat and on sledges, then got them up with ramps and levers. It took about 20 years. Scientists still don't agree on exactly what the ramps looked like.

visual.what: Huy, Hùng, Bối and little Beo stand in the bright studio in front of a huge picture of the Great Pyramid in the desert. Bối points up with wide eyes, and Beo is on tiptoe.

parts.text: Huy, this pyramid is gigantic! How did people build it without trucks or cranes?
Maybe a giant built it!
Great question, Bối. Here is a surprise. It was built more than 4,500 years ago, and it has about 2,300,000 stone blocks!

visual.what: Huy talks to the camera. Behind him, Hùng sits in a cardboard box painted like a time machine, and its paper dial falls off.

parts.text: Today we find out how the Egyptians cut the stones, moved them, lifted them up, and who did all that hard work. Let's go back in time!
Time machine ready! Oops, the dial fell off. We'll just pretend.

visual.what: Bối has a thought bubble with a crowd of sad, tired workers. Beo has a thought bubble with a hundred little toy robots carrying blocks.

parts.text: I know! Slaves built it. Lots of them, forced to work.
I think a hundred robots did it!
Good guesses, both of you. Robots weren't invented yet, Beo. But Bối, your guess is very sensible. Even the ancient Greeks believed it, long after the pyramid was built.

visual.what: Archaeologists with brushes kneel in the sand near the pyramid, gently uncovering simple stone graves. A sign says 1990.

parts.text: But in 1990, archaeologists found the workers' graves near the pyramid. Archaeologists are scientists who dig up clues from the past. The clues show the builders were workers who got paid. Some worked as a kind of tax, which means paying the king with work instead of money.
So they were builders with a real job?
Exactly! And how they did it is a story in four steps.

visual.what: A simple map of Egypt with the river Nile. Giza is marked with a pyramid, Tura across the river with white stone, and Aswan far to the south with pink granite. A small crown labelled Khufu sits by the pyramid.

parts.text: The pyramid was built for a king called Khufu. Egyptian kings were called pharaohs. Most of the stone came from right next to the building site. Fine white limestone came from Tura, across the river Nile. Very hard granite came from Aswan, far to the south.

visual.what: A copper chisel, a copper drill and a copper saw, each labelled, next to a limestone wall in a quarry. Hùng holds up a toy chisel.

parts.text: A place where people cut stone out of the ground is called a quarry. Workers cut the limestone with copper tools, like chisels, drills and saws.
Copper? Isn't copper quite soft?
Plain copper is. But theirs had another material mixed in, so it was harder, and hammering it made it harder still.

visual.what: A worker saws a granite block, with tiny sand grains drawn under the blade and an arrow saying sand does the scratching. In a corner, Hùng rubs a pebble with sandpaper, looking tired.

parts.text: What about the super hard granite?
Copper alone can't cut granite. So workers pounded it with an even harder stone, and sawed it with sand under the blade. The tiny sand grains did the scratching. It took a very long time!
I rubbed this pebble with sandpaper for a whole minute. Look, one tiny scratch!

visual.what: A big limestone block on one side of a balance and a family car on the other. The block side is lower, labelled about 2.5 tonnes.

parts.text: Most blocks weighed about 2.5 tonnes. That's heavier than a family car! A few giant granite blocks were much heavier.
Heavier than our car?
Yes, Beo! Step one takeaway. Copper tools, hard stones and sand turned rock into blocks.

visual.what: Explorers with torches in a cave find old rolled-up papyrus pages. A sign says Wadi al-Jarf, 2013, and the pages are labelled Diary of Merer.

parts.text: How do we know how the stones travelled? In 2013, scientists found old writings in a cave in Egypt. They are the diary of an official named Merer, written more than 4,500 years ago.
Does it say what he had for lunch?
Sadly not! But it says his team took limestone blocks from Tura to Giza by boat.

visual.what: Wooden boats carrying white blocks float along the blue river Nile, with an arrow from Tura to Giza. A tiny truck with a cross shows there were no trucks.

parts.text: Boats were the trucks of ancient Egypt, and the river Nile was the big road. A heavy block is much easier to move floating on water than dragged across the desert.
A boat for rocks!

visual.what: A block on a wooden sledge, labelled sledge, ropes and wet sand. A team pulls the ropes while one worker pours water in front. Hùng holds up a small wooden toy sled.

parts.text: I brought a sled! It's a toy one, though.
Perfect, Hùng. On land, blocks rode on a sledge. A sledge is a wooden sled, like a snow sled but with no snow. Teams pulled it with ropes. Scientists think water was poured in front to help it slide.

visual.what: Eight cartoon workers in a row pull one block on a sledge, each numbered 1 to 8. Next to them, Bối poses in a football shirt.

parts.text: How many people did it take to pull one block?
One expert worked out that about eight workers could move a block of about 2,750 kilograms on a sledge, if the track was made slippery.
Only eight? My football team could do that!
Maybe, after a lot of practice!

visual.what: Huy talks to the camera next to a small picture of a boat and a sledge with a tick beside each.

parts.text: Step two takeaway. Boats carried the stones along the river, and sledges slid them over land.

visual.what: The new pyramid, labelled about 146 metres, stands next to a football pitch stood up on its end. The pyramid is taller.

parts.text: Now for the hardest part. When it was new, the pyramid was about 146 metres tall. That's taller than a football pitch is long, if you stood the pitch on its end!
So how do you get a heavy block all the way up there?

visual.what: A simple ramp leaning against the side of a half-built pyramid, labelled ramp. A team drags a sledge up it. Beo looks at it with a big smile.

parts.text: Most experts think the answer starts with ramps. A ramp is a sloping path, like a slide you walk up. Builders dragged the sledges up ramps to the higher layers. Remains of small ramps have been found at the Great Pyramid.
A slide! Can I slide down it?
These slides were only for stones, Beo.

visual.what: Hùng puts a ruler over a pencil and presses one end down to lift a book on the other end. The book tips over and lands on his foot, and he laughs.

parts.text: Ramps were probably helped by levers. A lever is a long, strong pole. Push down on one end, and the other end lifts something heavy a little bit. Lever, nudge, lever again, and the block slowly creeps into place.
Look, I pushed down and the book went up! And then it went down. On my foot.

visual.what: Three small pyramids side by side. One has a huge straight ramp with a red cross, one has a zigzag ramp, and one has a ramp spiralling around the outside, each with a question mark.

parts.text: So what did the ramp look like?

Here's a secret. Scientists still don't agree! One giant straight ramp would have been enormous, so most experts think it wasn't that. Some think of a zigzag ramp up one side, or a ramp that spirals round the outside.

visual.what: A see-through pyramid showing a ramp spiralling up inside, plus a short ramp outside at the bottom for big blocks. A label says Jean-Pierre Houdin's idea.

parts.text: A French architect called Jean-Pierre Houdin has another idea. He thinks a ramp spiralled up inside the pyramid, plus a ramp outside for the big blocks lower down.
A ramp hidden inside? That's sneaky!
Maybe they used different tricks at different heights. Scientists are still hunting for clues.

visual.what: Huy talks to the camera next to a ramp and a lever drawing, with a big question mark over the ramp.

parts.text: Step three takeaway. Ramps and levers got the blocks up, but exactly what the ramps looked like is still a mystery.

visual.what: Long trenches dug in the ground and filled with still water, with workers marking a straight line at the water's edge. A label says still water lies flat.

parts.text: Before the first block, the ground had to be really flat. Some experts think workers dug long trenches and filled them with water. Still water lies flat, so they could mark a level line.
Like my bathwater when I stop splashing!
I never stop splashing!

visual.what: A crowd of little workers labelled about 20,000 workers next to a calendar showing about 20 years. Behind them are rows of tents by the pyramid.

parts.text: Experts think about 20,000 workers built it, and it took about 20 years. They camped near the pyramid. They were skilled, which means they were very good at their jobs, like cutting, dragging and measuring.

visual.what: Zooming into the inside of the pyramid. Rough blocks with gaps between them, and the gaps filled with small broken stones and white plaster, labelled rubble and gypsum.

parts.text: The blocks inside weren't perfect. They were roughly cut. Workers filled the gaps with rubble, which means broken bits of stone, and a kind of plaster called gypsum.

visual.what: On the left, the pyramid long ago, covered in smooth shining white stones. On the right, the pyramid today with its rough steps and a few white stones left at the bottom.

parts.text: Last came the outside. Smooth white stones covered the whole pyramid. Most of them are gone now, but you can still see some around the bottom.
So it used to be a giant smooth white triangle!
Like a big snow mountain!

visual.what: Huy talks to the camera. A small picture behind him shows a man named Hemiunu holding a plan on papyrus.

parts.text: All this needed a planner. Experts think it may have been Hemiunu, the king's top helper.
Step four takeaway. Thousands of paid, skilled workers and lots of smart planning built it over about 20 years.

visual.what: A big clock and a counter showing about 300 blocks a day. Hùng hurries to stack toy blocks while Bối flops on a cushion.

parts.text: Imagine if you had to place 2,300,000 blocks in 20 years. That's about 300 blocks every single day. If you worked ten hours a day, you'd need to place a block about every two minutes!
I'll try with toy blocks. One, two... oh no, my tower fell!
I'm tired just hearing that.

visual.what: In a sandbox, Hùng has a small box full of pebbles with a string tied on. He pulls it over dry sand while a grown-up watches.

parts.text: Want to test the sledge idea? Hùng will show you.
In a sandbox, with a grown-up, put some pebbles in a small box and tie on a string. Pull it over dry sand. Feel how hard it is.

visual.what: Hùng sprinkles a little water from a small cup onto the sand in front of the box. Bối holds the string ready, and Beo watches closely.

parts.text: Then sprinkle a little water on the sand and pull again.
Will it feel easier or harder? I'm going to find out!
Me too! I pull!
Tell us what you find. Testing ideas is exactly what scientists do.

visual.what: Four small pictures joined by arrows. Copper tools cutting stone, a boat on the Nile, a sledge on sand, and blocks going up a ramp to a finished pyramid.

parts.text: So, how was it built? Thousands of paid workers cut stones with copper tools and sand, moved them by boat and sledge, and got them up with ramps and levers, over about 20 years.

visual.what: A long timeline with the Great Pyramid as the tallest building at the start. A banner over it says tallest for over 3,800 years.

parts.text: Here's a fun fact. The Great Pyramid was the tallest building in the world for over 3,800 years!
Nobody built anything taller for 3,800 years? Wow!

visual.what: All four wave goodbye in the studio. Hùng holds up a papyrus plant, and a big button on screen says Subscribe to Ask Huy.

parts.text: Next time, how did the ancient Egyptians make paper from a plant?
Paper from a plant? I have to know!
Paper grows?
Subscribe to Ask Huy so you don't miss it. Bye for now!

facts.claim: The Great Pyramid was built more than 4,500 years ago.
The pyramid's core is about 2,300,000 blocks of limestone and granite.
The ancient Greeks, long after it was built, believed the pyramids were built by slaves.
Workers' graves found near the pyramid in 1990 show the builders were paid workers, not slaves.
Some workers worked for a salary and some as a form of tax payment.
The pyramid was built for the pharaoh Khufu.
Local limestone was used for the body, fine limestone from Tura for the casing, and granite from near Aswan.
Stone was cut with copper chisels, drills and saws; the copper was arsenical copper, harder than plain copper and made harder by hammering.
Granite could not be cut with copper alone and was pounded with dolerite and sawn with sand as an abrasive.
Most blocks weighed about 2.5 tonnes; some were much heavier.
The diary of Merer, found in 2013 in a cave at Wadi al-Jarf and written more than 4,500 years ago, describes moving limestone from Tura to Giza by boat.
Blocks were moved on sledges, likely made slippery with water.
About eight workers could move a 2,750 kg block on a lubricated sledge (Denys Stocks' estimate).
The pyramid was about 146.5 metres tall when built.
Most Egyptologists think ramps were used, helped by levers; remains of small ramps have been found at the Great Pyramid.
Egyptians used simple machines such as the ramp and the lever.
Scientists disagree about the ramp shape; a giant straight ramp is widely rejected; zigzag and spiral ramps have been proposed.
Jean-Pierre Houdin proposed an internal spiral ramp plus an external ramp for bigger blocks lower down.
The foundation may have been levelled using water-filled trenches.
Construction is thought to have taken about 20,000 workers and about 20 years.
Workers were skilled and camped near the pyramids.
Core stones were roughly cut and gaps were filled with gypsum and rubble.
The pyramid was covered by smooth white stones; some can still be seen around the base.
It may have been built by Khufu's vizier Hemiunu.
The Great Pyramid was the tallest building in the world for over 3,800 years.
Egyptians made paper from the papyrus plant.

description: How did people build the Great Pyramid of Giza more than 4,500 years ago, without trucks or cranes? Join Huy, Hùng, Bối and Beo to learn how paid, skilled workers cut stone with copper tools and sand, moved it by boat and sledge, and lifted it with ramps and levers. There's also a safe sandbox test to try with a grown-up. For curious kids aged 6–12, based on what archaeologists know today, including the parts that are still a mystery.

cast.role: the host (25): curious, warm, a little funny; explains

cast.name: Hùng
cast.role: Huy's younger brother (21), his hands-on assistant: sets up and runs the experiments and demos, brings things, now and then a funny little mishap

cast.name: Bối
cast.role: an 8-year-old girl who asks, guesses and tries things

cast.name: Beo
cast.role: Bối's 5-year-old little brother: curious, makes funny innocent guesses
